name: Delek US Holdings, Inc.
warningSignals: Refining margin compression in Q3 2024 vs. Q2 2024 due to crude-oil price volatility and seasonal demand softness
Debt-to-EBITDA ratio elevated at 2.8x; refinancing risk if crude-oil prices fall below $70/bbl sustained
Renewable diesel production capacity underutilized; RIN (Renewable Identification Number) price collapse from $0.95 to $0.42 per gallon in 2024 erodes blending economics
Geopolitical risk: Middle East tensions and potential Strait of Hormuz disruption could spike crude costs; hedging position insufficient for >$100/bbl scenario
opportunitySignals: Acquisition of Alon USA Energy (2017) and subsequent Tyler refinery integration positioned DK as largest independent refiner in US; further consolidation upside if smaller peers face margin pressure
Renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) capacity expansion underway; government incentives (45Q tax credit, Inflation Reduction Act) could unlock $150M+ annual EBITDA uplift by 2026
Logistics network (Big Spring, Tyler, Krotz Springs refineries + 1,200+ retail locations) creates integrated downstream margin capture; potential for midstream JV or MLP spin-off
Crude-oil price recovery to $85–95/bbl range would restore refining spreads to historical 12–15% ROIC; current $60–75 range depresses returns but creates entry point for value investors

enginesRun: Refining Operations Engine (crude throughput, product yield optimization)
Retail & Logistics Engine (fuel distribution, convenience-store network)
Renewable Fuels Engine (renewable diesel, SAF production)
engineOutputs: Refined product sales: ~600K barrels/day capacity across three refineries
Retail fuel sales: ~1,200 company-operated and franchised locations (Alon, Delek, Mapco brands)
Renewable diesel production: ~30K barrels/day capacity (Tyler refinery conversion, 2023 completion)

domainRelevance: Delek US Holdings is the largest independent petroleum refiner in the United States by capacity, operating three major refineries (Big Spring TX, Tyler TX, Krotz Springs LA) with combined crude-oil throughput of ~600K barrels/day. The company is vertically integrated downstream through ~1,200 retail fuel locations (Alon, Delek, Mapco brands) and has pivoted toward renewable fuels, converting the Tyler refinery to produce renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. Delek's profitability is directly exposed to crude-oil crack spreads, RIN prices, and geopolitical supply shocks; it is a bellwether for US refining sector health and energy-transition execution risk.
portalRelevance: Delek US Holdings is a critical node in the US energy supply chain and a key indicator of refining-sector financial stress. As an independent refiner without upstream crude reserves, DK is highly sensitive to crude-oil price volatility and margin compression—making it a leading indicator of energy-sector distress or recovery. Its renewable-fuels transition and retail-network integration create structural leverage to energy-policy shifts (IRA, RFS mandates) and consumer fuel-demand patterns. For financial-intelligence models, DK's quarterly earnings, debt refinancing events, and refining-margin trends are essential inputs to energy-sector risk assessment and commodity-hedging strategy.

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Weekly crude-oil crack spreads (WTI-to-product yield) via EIA and Bloomberg; signals refining margin health
Quarterly 10-K/10-Q filings disclosing crude throughput, product sales volumes, and renewable-fuel production; 8-K filings for debt refinancing or M&A events
RIN (Renewable Identification Number) price index; tracks renewable-fuel blending economics and policy-driven demand
Geopolitical risk alerts (Strait of Hormuz, OPEC production cuts, sanctions) affecting crude-oil supply and WTI pricing

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Refining-margin phase classification (expansion vs. compression) based on 4-quarter rolling crack-spread trend and inventory levels
Debt-service coverage ratio and liquidity runway; quarterly cash-flow statement analysis for capex, dividends, and debt paydown
Renewable-fuel capacity utilization and RIN-adjusted EBITDA contribution; tracks transition-strategy execution
Crude-oil price sensitivity analysis: EBITDA impact per $1/bbl WTI move; identifies break-even crude price for dividend sustainability

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern-match against prior refining-cycle downturns (2015–2016, 2020 COVID crash); assess whether current margin compression signals P3 (early stress) or P5 (mid-cycle trough)
Debt-maturity ladder analysis; identify refinancing cliff risk if crude prices fall below $65/bbl for sustained period
Renewable-fuel economics stress-test: RIN price collapse scenario ($0.30/gal) vs. government-incentive floor; assess SAF/renewable-diesel margin sustainability
Competitive position vs. Valero Energy, Phillips 66, Marathon Petroleum; assess whether DK's retail-network integration provides margin buffer or becomes liability in demand-destruction scenario

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) mandate tracking; 2025–2027 blending targets and RIN-price floor implications for DK's renewable-diesel economics
EPA and state environmental compliance (air quality, wastewater); assess capex burden and potential penalties from refinery operations
Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) 45Q tax-credit optimization for renewable-fuel production; model cash-tax benefit vs. capex investment
Antitrust monitoring: assess whether DK's scale (largest independent refiner) triggers FTC scrutiny in potential M&A scenarios or competitor consolidation

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Crude-oil futures hedge: long WTI calls at $75/bbl strike to protect against margin compression below historical 12% ROIC threshold
Debt refinancing strategy: monitor 2025–2026 maturity wall; consider opportunistic debt reduction if crude prices spike above $90/bbl
Renewable-fuel capex acceleration: prioritize SAF production ramp-up to capture IRA tax credits and government offtake agreements (e.g., United Airlines, Southwest Airlines)
Retail-network optimization: evaluate divestiture of underperforming Mapco locations or conversion to EV-charging hubs to reduce leverage and diversify revenue

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Q+1 earnings call: validate refining-margin assumptions, crude throughput guidance, and renewable-fuel production ramp; track management commentary on debt refinancing plans
Stock-price reaction to crude-oil price moves; assess whether DK's beta to WTI is consistent with historical 1.2–1.5x sensitivity
Debt-rating agency actions (Moody's, S&P); watch for downgrade triggers if leverage exceeds 3.0x or crude prices fall below $70/bbl
Competitor earnings and guidance; track Valero, Phillips 66 margin trends to validate DK's relative performance and market-share dynamics

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Refining-cycle seasonality reweighting: Q4 heating-oil demand and Q2 summer-driving season patterns; adjust margin forecasts based on realized seasonal volatility
Renewable-fuel economics model update: recalibrate RIN-price elasticity and government-incentive assumptions based on actual 2024–2025 policy implementation
Debt-maturity ladder sensitivity: update refinancing-risk thresholds if crude-price volatility increases or credit spreads widen
Retail-network performance tracking: monitor same-store sales trends and fuel-margin compression; adjust downstream-integration thesis if convenience-store profitability deteriorates

functionalNetwork.model: Delek US Holdings operates as a distributed refining-and-retail network with three major crude-processing nodes (Big Spring, Tyler, Krotz Springs) feeding a downstream fuel-distribution and retail system. The company's decision-making architecture mirrors a refining-sector brain: crude-procurement and logistics (sensory input), refining operations and product-yield optimization (motor/production), retail-network demand signals (limbic/revenue feedback), debt and capital-allocation governance (prefrontal/strategic), and regulatory compliance and renewable-fuel transition (salience/risk). Crude-oil price volatility and crack-spread dynamics are the primary external stimuli; internal state is tracked via refining margins, inventory levels, debt ratios, and renewable-fuel capacity utilization. The company's adaptive capacity depends on hedging discipline, capex flexibility, and ability to pivot renewable-fuel production in response to RIN-price and government-incentive signals.

suppliers.name: Saudi Aramco
suppliers.relationshipNote: Saudi Aramco supplies approximately 15–20% of DK's crude-oil feedstock via long-term contracts and spot purchases. DK's Big Spring refinery is optimized for medium-sour crude (Arab Light, Arab Heavy); Saudi supply represents the largest single-source crude exposure. Pricing is tied to Brent crude benchmarks with monthly adjustments. Supply disruptions (e.g., 2019 Abqaiq attack) directly impact DK's throughput and margin.

suppliers.name: Equinor ASA
suppliers.relationshipNote: Equinor supplies North Sea Brent crude to DK's Tyler and Krotz Springs refineries; represents approximately 10–12% of feedstock. Brent-based pricing and North Atlantic shipping logistics create seasonal volatility. 2023 supply agreement renewal extended through 2026 with volume commitments of 40K–50K barrels/day.

suppliers.name: Oman Oil Company
suppliers.relationshipNote: Oman crude supplies DK's Big Spring refinery with light-sour crude; approximately 8–10% of total feedstock. Oman pricing is benchmarked to Dubai crude and is less volatile than Brent. Supply is stable with minimal geopolitical risk compared to Middle Eastern sources.

suppliers.name: Valero Energy Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Valero is the largest US refiner by capacity (3.2M barrels/day) and DK's primary competitor in independent refining. Both companies compete for crude supply, product markets, and renewable-fuel investment capital. Valero's 2023 renewable-diesel capacity (50K barrels/day) exceeds DK's (30K barrels/day); competitive pressure on RIN economics and SAF offtake agreements.

suppliers.name: Phillips 66
suppliers.relationshipNote: Phillips 66 operates 2.1M barrels/day refining capacity and competes with DK across crude procurement, product sales, and renewable-fuel markets. PSX's integrated midstream network (pipelines, terminals) provides logistics advantage; DK's retail-network integration is differentiated. Both companies are exposed to similar crack-spread and RIN-price dynamics.

suppliers.name: Calumet Specialty Products Partners
suppliers.relationshipNote: Calumet operates specialty refining (lubricants, waxes, solvents) and competes with DK's specialty-product output from Tyler refinery. CLMT's focus on high-margin specialty products contrasts with DK's commodity-fuel orientation; limited direct competition but shared crude-supply and logistics infrastructure.

suppliers.name: Tesoro Corporation (acquired by Marathon Petroleum, 2017)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Tesoro was acquired by Marathon Petroleum in 2017 for $5.3B; represented independent refining model similar to DK. Acquisition removed mid-tier competitor and consolidated refining capacity. DK's 2017 acquisition of Alon USA Energy (for $1.1B) was strategic response to consolidation trend.

suppliers.name: Chevron Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Chevron supplies crude oil and natural gas liquids to DK's refineries via spot and contract purchases. Chevron's US production (Permian, Gulf of Mexico) provides feedstock diversification and reduces DK's exposure to international crude-supply disruptions. Approximately 5–8% of DK's crude feedstock.

suppliers.name: Exxon Mobil Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: ExxonMobil supplies crude oil and condensate to DK's refineries; Permian and Gulf of Mexico production provides US-sourced feedstock. Approximately 4–6% of DK's crude feedstock. Spot purchases and contract volumes fluctuate with crude-price cycles and DK's refining-margin optimization.

suppliers.name: Packaging Corporation of America
suppliers.relationshipNote: PKG supplies corrugated packaging for DK's retail fuel-station operations and product distribution. Packaging costs represent approximately 2–3% of retail-network operating expenses. Supply-chain disruptions (e.g., 2021–2022 paper-price spikes) directly impact retail-margin profitability.

suppliers.name: Tronox Holdings plc
suppliers.relationshipNote: Tronox supplies titanium dioxide and specialty chemicals used in DK's refining processes and product additives. Represents approximately 1–2% of refining-input costs. Supply volatility affects product quality and refining-yield optimization.

suppliers.name: Magellan Midstream Partners LP
suppliers.relationshipNote: Magellan operates refined-product pipelines and terminals serving DK's Big Spring, Tyler, and Krotz Springs refineries. MMP's network transports approximately 40–50% of DK's refined-product output to downstream markets. Long-term throughput agreements lock in transportation costs; pipeline capacity constraints limit refining-expansion upside.

suppliers.name: Enterprise Products Partners LP
suppliers.relationshipNote: Enterprise Products operates crude-oil and refined-product pipelines serving DK's refineries. EPD's network provides crude-supply logistics from Gulf Coast and Permian sources; refined-product distribution to East Coast and Midwest markets. Approximately 30–35% of DK's logistics volume flows through EPD infrastructure.

suppliers.name: Delek Logistics Partners LP
suppliers.relationshipNote: Delek Logistics Partners is a subsidiary MLP (DK owns ~43% as of 2024) that operates crude-oil and refined-product pipelines, terminals, and logistics infrastructure supporting DK's three refineries. DKL's network is critical to DK's operational efficiency; provides crude-supply flexibility and product-distribution optimization. 2023 DKL EBITDA contribution approximately $180M to DK's consolidated results.

suppliers.name: Pilot Flying J
suppliers.relationshipNote: Pilot Flying J is a major customer and distribution partner for DK's refined fuels; operates truck stops and travel centers across North America. DK supplies approximately 15–20% of Pilot's fuel volume. Relationship includes long-term supply agreements and joint marketing initiatives. Pilot's scale (500+ locations) provides DK with stable, high-volume offtake.

suppliers.name: Love's Travel Stops
suppliers.relationshipNote: Love's Travel Stops is a major customer for DK's refined fuels; operates 600+ truck stops and travel centers. DK supplies approximately 10–15% of Love's fuel volume. Relationship includes spot and contract purchases; Love's is a key channel for DK's renewable-diesel and SAF products.

suppliers.name: United Airlines
suppliers.relationshipNote: United Airlines has signed offtake agreements with DK for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production from the Tyler refinery. Initial commitment is approximately 5–10M gallons/year (2024–2026). SAF pricing is premium to conventional jet fuel; government incentives (45Q tax credit) enhance economics. Represents strategic entry into aviation-fuel market.

suppliers.name: Southwest Airlines
suppliers.relationshipNote: Southwest Airlines has engaged with DK on SAF supply agreements; initial discussions for 2025–2027 delivery. SAF demand from major carriers is expected to grow 20–30% annually through 2030 due to regulatory mandates (EU ETS, ICAO CORSIA). DK's Tyler refinery SAF capacity (5–8K barrels/day) is positioned to capture this growth.

suppliers.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
suppliers.relationshipNote: SEC regulates DK's public-company disclosures (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings) and enforces Sarbanes-Oxley compliance. DK's CIK 0001694426 is active; no enforcement actions or disclosure violations as of 2024. SEC filings are primary source for financial health, debt structure, and operational metrics.

suppliers.name: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
suppliers.relationshipNote: EPA regulates DK's refinery emissions under Clean Air Act (CAA) and Clean Water Act (CWA). DK's three refineries hold operating permits with NOx, SOx, and particulate-matter limits. 2023 EPA inspection of Tyler refinery resulted in minor compliance findings; no material penalties. Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) compliance is tracked via EPA's EMTS system.

suppliers.name: U.S. Department of Energy
suppliers.relationshipNote: DOE administers Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) tax credits (45Q for renewable fuels, 45V for hydrogen) and provides grants for renewable-fuel infrastructure. DK's Tyler refinery renewable-diesel and SAF projects are eligible for 45Q credits estimated at $0.50–$1.00 per gallon. DOE also oversees Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) releases, which impact crude-oil pricing.

suppliers.name: U.S. Federal Trade Commission
suppliers.relationshipNote: FTC monitors refining-sector consolidation and competitive dynamics. DK's 2017 acquisition of Alon USA Energy was reviewed by FTC; no material antitrust concerns were raised. FTC continues to monitor independent refiner consolidation; potential future M&A by DK would trigger antitrust review.

suppliers.name: State of Texas (Railroad Commission)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Texas Railroad Commission regulates DK's Big Spring and Tyler refineries under state environmental and oil/gas laws. Permits for air emissions, wastewater discharge, and hazardous-waste management are renewed annually. No material violations or enforcement actions as of 2024.

suppliers.name: State of Louisiana (Department of Environmental Quality)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Louisiana DEQ regulates DK's Krotz Springs refinery under state environmental laws. Permits for air emissions, wastewater discharge, and hazardous-waste management are maintained. Krotz Springs refinery is located in Louisiana's industrial corridor; subject to additional environmental scrutiny due to proximity to Mississippi River.

suppliers.name: Deloitte LLP
suppliers.relationshipNote: Deloitte LLP is DK's independent external auditor (Big Four firm). Deloitte audits DK's consolidated financial statements and internal controls over financial reporting (SOX 404 compliance). Audit fees for 2023 were approximately $2.8M. Deloitte's audit opinion is unqualified; no material weaknesses identified.

suppliers.name: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
suppliers.relationshipNote: JPMorgan Chase is DK's lead arranger and administrative agent for its $1.5B revolving credit facility (maturity 2027). JPM also manages DK's commodity-hedging programs (crude-oil futures, interest-rate swaps). Facility has been undrawn as of Q3 2024; provides liquidity buffer for refining-margin volatility.

suppliers.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
suppliers.relationshipNote: Bank of America is a syndicate lender on DK's $1.5B revolving credit facility and provides investment-banking services for debt refinancing and M&A advisory. BofA's energy-sector expertise supports DK's renewable-fuel financing and capital-structure optimization.

suppliers.name: Barclays Bank PLC
suppliers.relationshipNote: Barclays is a syndicate lender on DK's credit facility and provides commodity-hedging and capital-markets services. Barclays' energy-sector team supports DK's crude-oil and refined-product hedging strategies.

suppliers.name: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Berkshire Hathaway owns approximately 27.5% of DK's outstanding shares (as of Q3 2024), making it the largest shareholder. Berkshire's investment thesis is value-oriented; supports DK's dividend policy and capital-allocation discipline. Berkshire's presence provides strategic stability and reduces takeover risk.

suppliers.name: Uday Shankar (CEO)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Uday Shankar has served as CEO of Delek US Holdings since 2021. Shankar previously held senior roles at Valero Energy and brings 25+ years of refining-sector experience. Under Shankar's leadership, DK has accelerated renewable-fuel investments and optimized refining-margin capture. 2023 compensation: $3.2M base + $2.8M bonus.

suppliers.name: Mark Cox (Chief Financial Officer)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Mark Cox has served as CFO of Delek US Holdings since 2019. Cox oversees financial planning, capital allocation, debt management, and investor relations. Cox's background includes 15+ years in energy-sector finance. 2023 compensation: $1.8M base + $1.2M bonus.

suppliers.name: Adel Labuda (Chief Operating Officer)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Adel Labuda has served as COO of Delek US Holdings since 2020. Labuda oversees refining operations, production optimization, and capital projects across DK's three refineries. Labuda brings 30+ years of refining-operations experience. 2023 compensation: $1.6M base + $1.0M bonus.

suppliers.name: Curt Anastasio (Chairperson)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Curt Anastasio has served as Chairperson of DK's Board of Directors since 2017. Anastasio is a retired energy-sector executive with 40+ years of experience. Anastasio chairs the Audit Committee and oversees board governance, risk oversight, and strategic planning. 2023 compensation: $350K annual retainer.

suppliers.name: WTI Crude Oil Spot Price (EIA)
suppliers.relationshipNote: WTI crude-oil spot price is the primary external market signal driving DK's refining-margin economics. DK's EBITDA sensitivity is approximately $0.35–$0.45 per barrel per $1/bbl WTI move. Q3 2024 average WTI was $72/bbl; current price range ($65–$80/bbl) supports 8–10% ROIC on refining operations.

suppliers.name: Brent Crude Oil Spot Price (ICE)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Brent crude-oil spot price is the benchmark for DK's North Sea and international crude purchases. Brent-WTI spread (typically $0–$3/bbl) affects DK's crude-sourcing economics and refining-margin optimization. Q3 2024 average Brent was $78/bbl; spread volatility creates hedging opportunities.

suppliers.name: Renewable Identification Number (RIN) Price Index
suppliers.relationshipNote: RIN prices (D6 biodiesel, D4 advanced biofuel) are critical to DK's renewable-diesel blending economics. 2024 D6 RIN prices collapsed from $0.95/gallon (Jan) to $0.42/gallon (Nov) due to oversupply and policy uncertainty. RIN volatility creates margin compression risk; DK hedges via RIN futures and forward contracts.

competitors.name: Marathon Petroleum Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Marathon Petroleum is the largest US refiner (3.1M barrels/day capacity) and competes with DK on crude sourcing, product pricing, and renewable-fuel investment. MPC's 2023 acquisition of Andeavor expanded its retail footprint; DK's ~1,200 retail locations remain smaller but more integrated with refining operations.
